CITY COUNCIL OF MONTEREY PARK
  THE CITY COUNCIL ACTING ON BEHALF OF THE SUCCESSOR AGENCY OF THE FORMER
 REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY, THE HOUSING AUTHORITY, THE MONTEREY PARK FINANCING
  AUTHORITY AND THE MONTEREY PARK GEOLOGIC HAZARD ABATEMENT DISTRICT
  AGENDA

  REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  MONTEREY PARK CITY HALL COUNCIL CHAMBERS
  320 W. NEWMARK AVENUE, MONTEREY PARK, CA 91754

  Wednesday
  June 21, 2023
  6:30 p.m.

  MISSION STATEMENT
  The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent services
  to enhance the quality of life for our entire community.

  LAND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
  We would like to acknowledge that the land we inhabit today was once known as
  Tovangaar, the home of the Gabrieleño-Tongva people. We show our respect to the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, as well as all Indigenous people, past, present, and future,
  and honor their labor as original caretakers of this land. We commit to uplifting the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, invite you to acknowledge the history, and join us in caring
  for this land.

GENERAL INFORMATION
Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at 320
West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s website
at http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/AgendaCenter/City-Council-17.

The public may watch the meeting live on the city’s cable channel MPKTV (AT&T U-verse, channel 99
or Charter Communications, channel 182) or by visiting the city’s website at
http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
You may speak up to 5 minutes on Agenda item. You may combine up to 2 minutes of time with another
person’s speaking. No person may speak more than a total of 10 minutes. The Mayor and City Council
may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. Written Communication will be accepted up to 24
hours before the meeting via email to mpclerk@montereypark.ca.gov.

Per the Americans with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting,
please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359 for reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a meeting.
Council Chambers are wheelchair accessible.

  It is recommended that the City Council consider:

  (2) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

 3-B.  RECOMMENDATIONS FOR ADOPTION OF FISCAL YEAR 2023-24 ANNUAL BUDGET
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Adopting by Resolution the City’s and Successor Agency’s Fiscal Year 2023-2024 Annual
  Budget as presented on May 24, 2023;
  (2) Adopting a Resolution approving the Citywide Combined Salary Schedule; and
  (3) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

  approved by the City Attorney with Chinatown Service Center to utilize the Sierra Vista
  Community Center as a temporary MPK Hope Resiliency Center to provide mental health

  Community Center until Antiterrorism Emergency Assistance Program (AEAP) grant funds

  Map No. 71473 in a form approved by the City Attorney;

3-K.  SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA EDISON 5-YEAR REVOCABLE SECONDARY LAND USE

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Martha Garcia, Director of Finance
 SUBJECT:  Recommendations for Adoption of Fiscal Year 2023-24 Annual Budget

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopting by Resolution the City’s and Successor Agency’s Fiscal Year 2023-
  2024 Annual Budget as presented on May 24, 2023;
  2. Adopting a Resolution approving the Citywide Combined Salary Schedule; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On May 24, 2023, the City Council conducted a public budget workshop regarding the
City’s current finances, projected revenues, and financial obligations. The budget for FY
2023-2024 presents a spending plan that anticipates $145.5 million in estimated
operating revenues and transfers-in; $27.5 million from grant advancements and fund
balance from all funds combined; and $173 million in operating, and capital improvements
expenditures and transfers-out. Financial matters, included the addition of staff, the
American Rescue Program Act funds, Community Development Department projects, the
Citywide compensation study, and all other goals and objectives associated with the City
budget, were presented and discussed at the workshop.
In addition, the City Council’s fiscal year 2023-2024 Strategic Plan Goals were added to
the budget document to provide a roadmap for prioritizing implementation of the specific
objectives that will be focused on during the budget cycle.

BACKGROUND:
Strategic planning is a method by which the City Council plans and prioritizes its goals in
a transparent and accountable manner. At a public meeting held on April 8, 2023, the City
Council and City’s management team met to discuss fiscal year 2023-2024 City Council
priorities and strategic plan goals. The Strategic Plan goals enables the City to efficiently
move the community forward by focusing on specific objectives during the fiscal
year. The Strategic Plan goals can be found on page B12 (and are also listed below) of
the fiscal year 2023-24 budget book and serves as a roadmap to guide the City’s vision
and helps to prioritize objective implementation. The City Council and staff uses the
Plan’s goals to align limited resources with prioritized initiatives, which connect to a
broader vision for our community’s future.

The Fiscal Year 2023-2024 Strategic Plan goals include:
  ❖ Sustainability
  ❖ Housing
  ❖ Public Safety & Homelessness
  ❖ MPK Healing – Community support resulting from the shooting incident
  ❖ City Property/Facilities
  ❖ Public Communications
  ❖ Economic Development
  ❖ Civic Engagement

On May 24, 2023, City Council conducted a public budget workshop wherein FY 2023-24
estimated revenues presented were $145.5 million, grant advancements and fund
balance were $27.5 million, and expenditures were $173 million. The workshop included
discussions on the addition of staff to the City’s employee roster, the American Rescue
Program Act funds and general fund supplement, the rebuilding of Community
Development Department and its projects, the Citywide compensation study, and all other
goals and objectives associated with the City budget.
The Citywide compensation study was presented to Council on April 5, 2023 in a receive
and file staff report. The FY 2023-2024 proposed budget includes cost associated with
bringing employee salaries below the median to the recommended median. Since most
bargaining units are currently under negotiation, it is recommended that the attached
combined salary schedule be approved to include adjusting hourly rates for the part-time
classifications due to the state minimum wage increases over the past few years which
has caused compaction with other part-time positions and bringing Executive and
unrepresented management to an average median. The City increased hourly rates for
the specific positions that were below the minimum wage by hiring the new staff at a
higher step in the salary range. By not adjusting the entire part-time salary ranges, over
the past two years it has caused compaction for entry level part-time positions making
similar hourly rates as skilled level part-time positions. For example, a new Recreation
Leader (no experience required) starts at $15.74/hr. based on the current salary schedule
and rate that is above minimum wage of $15.50/hr. and a new Senior Lifeguard (who is
required to have at least two certifications and experience to instruct swimming classes
to be qualified as a Senior lifeguard) starts at $15.58/hr. Taking this action will assist with
compaction issues and the negotiations of the remaining bargaining units. It will take
affect the first full pay period after July 1, 2023.

Therefore, the City’s FY 2023-2024 Operating, Debt and Capital Budget total is $173
million of which $61.8 million is in the General Fund, $27 million is for capital
improvements and $2.2 is for the Successor Agency enforceable obligations and
administration costs. A careful and methodical approach was taken in preparing the
budget consistent with City Council’s practice to exercise fiscal prudence with funding
requests and the preservation of the General Fund reserves. Departmental budget

   RESOLUTION NO.

  A RESOLUTION ADOPTING THE FISCAL YEAR 2023-2024 FINAL
  OPERATING, DEBT AND CAPITAL BUDGET FOR THE CITY OF
  MONTEREY PARK; THE SUCCESSOR AGENCY TO THE MONTEREY
  PARK REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY; THE MONTEREY PARK FINANCING
  AUTHORITY; THE MONTEREY PARK HOUSING AUTHORITY; AND THE
  GEOLOGIC HAZARD ABATEMENT DISTRICT

  The City Council for the City of Monterey Park and the City Council acting on
behalf of the Successor Agency (collectively referred to, for convenience, as the “City”)
does resolve as follows:

SECTION 1: FINDINGS. The City Council finds and declares as follows:

  A.  The City Council reviewed the proposed final Operating and Debt Budget
  (“Budget”) for the City and Capital Improvement Plan (“CIP”) for fiscal year
  2023-2024;

  B.  The Budget and CIP are based upon appropriate estimates and financial
  planning for the City’s operations, debt and capital improvements;

  C.  The City Council conducted public study sessions on May 24, 2023;

  D.  The City Council is fully informed regarding the City’s current finances,
  projected revenue, and financial obligations; and

  E.  It is in the public interest for the City Council to adopt the Budget and CIP
  as proposed by the City Manager.

SECTION 2: Adoption.  The Budget and the Capital Improvement Projects as
incorporated by reference to this Resolution are approved and adopted subject only to
the authorizations set forth below. Such approval and adoption includes, without
limitation, the Position Control Listing of Authorized Positions, Classification and
Compensation Plans set forth in the Budget which recognizes new classifications and
removes unused classifications.

SECTION 3: Appropriations Limit.

  A.  Article XIIIB of the California Constitution requires the City to set its
  Appropriations Limit on an annual basis;

  B.  The City’s Appropriations Limit may be adjusted annually based upon
  inflation and population growth.

  C.  The City Council may choose the method of calculating adjustments to the
  City’s Appropriations Limit on an annual basis. For inflation, pursuant to
  Article XIIIB, § 8(e)(2), adjustments to the Appropriations Limit may be

  jurisdiction or from the surrounding county.

  D.  Pursuant to Article XIIIB of the California Constitution, and those
  Government Code sections adopted pursuant to Article XIIIB, § 8(f), the
  City Council chooses to adjust the City’s Appropriations Limit by
  calculating inflation using the California per capita personal income growth
  and calculating population growth by using the percentage change in
  population in Los Angeles County.

  E.  As a result of the adjustments made to the City’s Appropriations Limit, the
  City Council sets the Appropriations Limit for fiscal year 2023-2024 at
  $109.5 million.

SECTION 4: Budget Appropriations. Based upon the Budget, the total General Fund
operating budget, including transfers, is $61.8 million. The Overall City Budget is $173
million including Capital Improvement Projects. The City Manager, or designee, is
authorized to implement the appropriations for City Departments.

SECTION 5: CIP Appropriations. Based upon the CIP, a total of $27 million is
appropriated for capital improvement projects for fiscal year 2023-2024. The City
Manager, or designee, is authorized to implement the CIP.

SECTION 6: Reappropriation. The City Manager, or designee, is authorized to
reappropriate any unused appropriations for capital projects, special projects, and grant
programs at the close of fiscal year 2023-2024 for the Budget and CIP.

SECTION 7: Fund Operating Reserves. The City Manager, or designee, may
appropriate any remaining revenues at the close of fiscal year 2023-2024 into the
applicable Fund operating reserve per Governmental Accounting Standards Board
(GASB) Statement No. 54.

SECTION 8: Budget Adjustments.  The Budget may be subsequently adjusted as
follows:

  A.  By majority vote of the City Council;

  B.  By the City Manager, or designee, for all appropriation transfers between
  programs and sections within a City department and between

  AGENDA ITEM NO: Consent Calendar - 3C

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Ron Bow, City Manager
 SUBJECT:  Continue to extend the existence of an employment emergency for the
  City of Monterey Park

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receiving and filing this report;
  2. Continuing to extend the existence of an employment emergency for the City of
  Monterey Park and authorizing the City Manager to take all practical actions
  needed to implement the efficient recruitment and retention of persons for
  employment; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The City continues to make progress on filling vacancies. Since April 2023, the City has
hired or promoted candidates to fill Public Works Maintenance Supervisor, two Financial
Analysts, Recreation Manager, Code Enforcement Officer, two Police Officers, and an
Economic Development Specialist.

There are 30 full-time positions in the recruitment process along with 18 part-time
recruitments. Staff recommends extending the employment emergency as the City is in
the process of revising the Personnel Rules and Regulations to assist with modifying
the recruitment processes and procedures and recruiting qualified candidates to fill the
Water division vacancies continues to be challenging in the current workforce market.

BACKGROUND:
The revision of the City Personnel Rules and Regulations is an overhaul of modifying
recruitment and human resources practices and procedures that were last updated in
2009. Since 2009, there have been changes in the law that have impacted practices and
procedures that need to be accounted for as well. Once the revisions are drafted, the
City needs to meet and confer with the associations over the recommended changes.
The meet and confer process can take time in order to allow the associations ample
review period of the document and then to discuss the impacts of the changes for each
association. With eight labor negotiations in process, that has delayed the Personnel

   RESOLUTION NO. 2022-R49

  A RESOLUTION ADOPTED BY THE CITY COUNCIL FOR THE CITY OF
  MONTEREY PARK DECLARING THE EXISTENCE OF A LOCAL
  EMERGENCY DUE TO LACK OF EMPLOYEES AND AUTHORIZING THE
  CITY MANAGER TO TAKE ALL REASONABLE ACTIONS TO ACCELERATE
  RECRUITMENT AND RETENTION OF PUBLIC EMPLOYEES.

  BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Monterey Park as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds as follows:

  A.  Since the City Council officially terminated the COVID-19 local emergency
  in April, the City took ambituous actions to restore pre-pandemic levels of
  municipal services;

  B.  In reviewing personnel data from just the last six months, however, it is
  apparent that the City is seriously short-staffed.

  C.  The City of Monterey Park has 325 full time staff positions of which nearly
  70 are currently vacant. Of these positions, multiple are critical to protecting
  public health and safety including, without limitation, Water Production
  Supervisor; Senior Water Production System Operator; Water Utility
  Maintenance Worker; Director of Public Works; Facilities Maintenance
  Supervisor; Finance Manager; Firefighter; Police Officer; Senior Accountant; and
  Lifeguard;

  D.  These are positions that directly respond to the public and/or essential to
  the smooth operation of municipal services including, for example, providing
  potable drinking water, and ensuring public safety;

  E.  The City Council notes that multiple sources of publicly available
  information (see, e.g., “Quantifying the Nation’s Workforce Crisis – State of
  American Business 2022 Update” [January 10, 2022] published by the United
  States Chamber of Commerce [www.uschamber.com/workforce/quantifying-the-
  nations-workforce-crisis-2022-state-of-american-business-update] and “COVID-

  ARTICLE 7 - GRIEVANCE PROCEDURE

A.  DEFINITIONS

  1.  A "grievance" is an allegation by a member or PCOA on behalf of specified unit
  members of the bargaining unit who have been adversely affected by an alleged
  violation of the specific provisions of this Memorandum of Understanding during its
  term, or an appeal of a disciplinary action decision by the City Manager.

  2.  A "disciplinary appeal" is a formal written objection or challenge to any disciplinary
  action as defined by the Personnel Rules and Regulations. The grievance procedure
  shall not be utilized by an employee to contest the content of a performance evaluation,
  verbal or written reprimands or other documentation regarding the employee's work
  performance yet which is not defined as "disciplinary action" by Rule XV of the City
  Personnel Rules and Regulations. A "disciplinary appeal" shall be filed after written
  receipt of the City Manager's decision, and shall constitute the sole and exclusive
  process of appeal. Such appeals shall be processed at Level IV, Arbitration.

  Discipline shall be imposed in such a manner as to not violate the FLSA with regard
  to “exempt” employees.

  3.  Disputes regarding jurisdiction (grievable of an issue) shall not be subject to resolution
  by the grievance procedure and instead, are subject to resolution by an arbitrator.

  4.  A "grievant" is any unit member or PCOA on behalf of specified unit members
  adversely affected by an alleged violation of the specific provisions of this MOU, or a
  punitive disciplinary action.

  5.  A "day" is any day in which the administrative offices of the City of Monterey Park
  are open for regularly scheduled business.

B.  GENERAL PROVISIONS

  a. Any unit member who believes he/she has a grievance which is an alleged

  2.  Level II - Formal Written Grievance

  a.  If the grievance is not resolved during the informal conference and the grievant

  problem is unacceptable; and (d) A listing of specific actions requested of the
  City which will remedy the grievance.

  b.  The Fire Chief or designated representative shall communicate his/her
  decision, in writing, to the grievant within ten (10) days after receiving the
  grievance.

  c.  Within the above time limits, either party may request a personal conference.

  3.  Level III - Appeal to the City Manager

  a.  If the grievant is not satisfied with the decision at Level II the grievant may,
  within ten (10) days of the receipt of the decision at Level II, appeal the
  decision to the City Manager. This statement shall include a copy of the
  original grievance and appeal, and a clear, concise statement of the reasons for
  the appeal.

  b.  The City Manager shall communicate the decision, in writing, to the grievant
  within ten (10) days. If the City Manager does not respond within the time
  limits provided, the grievant may appeal to the next level.

  4.  Level IV - Binding Arbitration

  a.  If the grievant is not satisfied with the decision at Level III, or if an employee
  wishes to appeal the disciplinary decision of the City Manager, the

  ARTICLE 7 - GRIEVANCE PROCEDURE

A.  DEFINITIONS

  1.  A "grievance" is an allegation by a member or PCOA on behalf of specified unit
  members of the bargaining unit who have been adversely affected by an alleged
  violation of the specific provisions of this Memorandum of Understanding during its
  term, or an appeal of a disciplinary action decision by the City Manager.

  2.  A "disciplinary appeal" is a formal written objection or challenge to any disciplinary
  action as defined by the Personnel Rules and Regulations. The grievance procedure
  shall not be utilized by an employee to contest the content of a performance evaluation,
  verbal or written reprimands or other documentation regarding the employee's work
  performance yet which is not defined as "disciplinary action" by Rule XV of the City
  Personnel Rules and Regulations. A "disciplinary appeal" shall be filed after written
  receipt of the City Manager's decision, and shall constitute the sole and exclusive
  process of appeal. Such appeals shall be processed at Level IV, Arbitration.

  Discipline shall be imposed in such a manner as to not violate the FLSA with regard
  to “exempt” employees.

  3.  Disputes regarding jurisdiction (grievable of an issue) shall not be subject to resolution
  by the grievance procedure and instead, are subject to resolution by an arbitrator.

  4.  A "grievant" is any unit member or PCOA on behalf of specified unit members
  adversely affected by an alleged violation of the specific provisions of this MOU, or a
  punitive disciplinary action.

  5.  A "day" is any day in which the administrative offices of the City of Monterey Park
  are open for regularly scheduled business.

B.  GENERAL PROVISIONS

C.  PROCEDURE - Grievances will be processed in accordance with the following procedures:

  1.  Level I - Informal Resolution

  a. Any unit member who believes he/she has a grievance which is an alleged
  violation of the specific provisions of this Memorandum of Understanding shall
  present the grievance orally to the Fire Chief within fifteen (15) days after the
  grievant knew, or reasonably should have known, of the circumstances which form

  and shall not be processed. The Fire Chief shall hold discussions and attempt to
  resolve the matter within ten (10) days after the presentation of the grievance. It
  is the intent of this informal meeting that at least one personal conference be held
  between the aggrieved employee and the Fire Chief.

  2.  Level II - Formal Written Grievance

  a.  If the grievance is not resolved during the informal conference and the grievant
  wishes to continue the grievance process, the grievant shall present the
  grievance in writing on the appropriate form to the Fire Chief within ten (10)
  days after conclusion of Level I. The written information shall include: (a) A
  description of the specific grounds of the grievance, including names, dates,
  and places necessary for a complete understanding of the grievance; (b) A
  listing of the provisions of this agreement which are alleged to have been
  violated; (c) A listing of the reasons why the Level I proposed resolution of the
  problem is unacceptable; and (d) A listing of specific actions requested of the
  City which will remedy the grievance.

  b.  The Fire Chief or designated representative shall communicate his/her
  decision, in writing, to the grievant within ten (10) days after receiving the
  grievance.

  c.  Within the above time limits, either party may request a personal conference.

  3.  Level III - Appeal to the City Manager

  a.  If the grievant is not satisfied with the decision at Level II the grievant may,
  within ten (10) days of the receipt of the decision at Level II, appeal the
  decision to the City Manager. This statement shall include a copy of the
  original grievance and appeal, and a clear, concise statement of the reasons for
  the appeal.

  b.  The City Manager shall communicate the decision, in writing, to the grievant
  within ten (10) days. If the City Manager does not respond within the time
  limits provided, the grievant may appeal to the next level.

  4.  Level IV - Binding Arbitration

  a.  If the grievant is not satisfied with the decision at Level III, or if an employee
  wishes to appeal the disciplinary decision of the City Manager, the
  grievant/employee may, within ten (10) days of the receipt of the decision,
  submit a request in writing to PCOA for arbitration of the dispute. Within
  twenty (20) days of the grievant's receipt of the decision at Level III, PCOA
  shall inform the City, in writing, of its intent to arbitrate. PCOA and the City
  shall attempt to agree upon an arbitrator. If no agreement can be reached, they
  shall request that the State Mediation and Conciliation Service supply a panel
  of seven (7) names of persons experienced in hearing grievances in cities.

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Authorizing Mayor to sign a letter on behalf of the City supporting Governor
  Newsom’s proposal for a 28th Amendment to the United States Constitution to help
  address America’s Gun Violence Crisis;
  2. Authorizing Mayor to sign a letter on behalf of the City supporting the Language
  Access to Gun Violence Prevention Strategies Act of 2023;
  3. Receiving and filing the firearm legislative update report; and
  4. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On January 21, 2023, the City of Monterey Park experienced a Mass Casualty Incident
(MCI) where 20 people were shot. Eleven of those community members died. As our
community struggles with the challenge of working through this tragedy, fellow citizens
and residents in California and the rest of the country continue to be confronted with
substantially similar MCIs.

State and federal legislation continues to be proposed to help reduce the likelihood that
other communities will suffer the same fate as Monterey Park and numerous other
communities across the United States.

As requested by City Council Members, it is recommended that the City Council consider
supporting Governor Newsom’s proposal for a 28th Amendment to the United States
Constitution to help address America’s gun violence crisis and supporting the Language
Access to Gun Violence Prevention Strategies Act of 2023.

Staff recommends City Council receive and file the firearm legislative update report.

BACKGROUND:
The circumstances of Monterey Park’s January 21st MCI are well-documented. It is not
necessary to get into specifics other than to state that 11 of our friends, neighbors, and

Governor Newsom’s 28th Amendment Proposal
The 28th Amendment will permanently protect four broadly supported gun safety
principles into the U.S. Constitution:

  •  Raising the federal minimum age to purchase a firearm from 18 to 21;
  •  Mandating universal background checks to prevent truly dangerous people from
  purchasing a gun that could be used in a crime;
  •  Instituting a reasonable waiting period for all gun purchases; and
  •  Barring civilian purchase of assault weapons that serve no other purpose than to
  kill as many people as possible in a short amount of time – weapons of war our
  nation’s founders never foresaw.

More information can be found at https://www.gov.ca.gov/2023/06/08/28th-amendment/.

Language Access to Gun Violence Prevention Strategies Act of 2023
U.S. Congress, Representative Judy Chu is seeking support for the Language Access to
Gun Violence Prevention Strategies Act of 2023.

A summary of the Bill’s intention is provided in the attached letter and describes that the
Language Access to Gun Violence Prevention Strategies Act of 2023 proposes to fill the
gaps in the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act by ensuring robust in-language materials,
outreach to LEP communities, and culturally competent education to community
providers and law enforcement. It would do so by:
  • Requiring competent, community reviewed, translations of all public facing
  resources provided by the Departments of Justice (DOJ) and Health and Human
  Services (HHS) related to gun violence prevention strategies.
  • Directing the Attorney General to ensure federal grant applications for funds
  related to the creation and implementation of extreme risk protection orders and
  other prevention efforts incorporate meaningful engagement with communities
  with high numbers of individuals with LEP.
  • Directing the Attorney General and Secretary of HHS to develop and implement
  a national public awareness campaign for federally supported gun violence
  prevention strategies and firearm ownership safety with a focus on outreach and
  engagement with LEP communities.

Endorsing Organizations: March For Our Lives
Dear Colleague:
The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, signed into law on June 25, 2022, provided funding for
states and localities to develop and implement “red flag laws” – which allow family members to
petition for the temporary removal of guns from a loved one’s home when someone is at
significant risk for self-harm or harming others. Red flag laws have deterred at least 58 potential
mass shootings and other types of gun violence in California alone, and nearly all states have
now applied for this grant funding.
Unfortunately, there are still gaps in ensuring ALL communities are made aware of how they can
participate in them. After the horrific mass shooting in Monterey Park, authorities learned that
there were individuals in the gunman’s life who knew that he was experiencing a life crisis and
isolating himself while stockpiling guns and ammunition. Unfortunately, due to lack of public
education coupled with linguistic and cultural barriers, none of these individuals were aware that
this was something that could have been reported to the police.
Outreach to communities on proven prevention strategies needs to be done in multiple languages,
including Mandarin, Cantonese, and Vietnamese, so that we can all help in preventing future gun
violence deaths. In addition, we know that there are proven firearm safety strategies such as safe
gun storage practices that are promoted to communities through the CDC. Unfortunately, these
strategies are also leaving out the same limited English proficient (LEP) communities.
My bill would fill these gaps by ensuring robust in-language materials, outreach to LEP
communities, and culturally competent education to community providers and law enforcement.
It would do so by:
  •  Requiring competent, community reviewed, translations of all public facing resources
  provided by the Departments of Justice (DOJ) and Health and Human Services (HHS)
  related to gun violence prevention strategies.

  •  Directing the Attorney General to ensure federal grant applications for funds related to
  the creation and implementation of extreme risk protection orders and other prevention
  efforts incorporate meaningful engagement with communities with high numbers of
  individuals with LEP.

  •  Directing the Attorney General and Secretary of HHS to develop and implement a
  national public awareness campaign for federally supported gun violence prevention
  strategies and firearm ownership safety with a focus on outreach and engagement with
  LEP communities.

Please reach out to Kristen Torres at Kristen.torres@mail.house.gov for questions or to sign on.
Sincerely,

BOARD/COMMISSION REVIEW:

The Planning Commission, at its April 25, 2023 meeting reviewed this ordinance. With a
unanimous vote, the Commission recommended to Council to adopt the draft Ordinance
amending regulations related to Density Bonus under ZCA-23-01.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

On May 17, 2023, the City Council by a unanimous vote, continued the item to June 7,
2022.

In March of 2022, the City Council categorized an update of the Density Bonus Ordinance
as a moderate priority. On November 2, 2022, City Council asked Staff to bring forward
an update to the Density Bonus Ordinance in coordination with the Inclusionary Housing
Ordinance. On November 16, 2022, the City Council amended and adopted the 2021-
2029 Housing Element that included Program 14: Affordable Housing Development
Incentives, which identified an objective to consider updating the City’s Density
Ordinance.

BACKGROUND:

A density bonus is an incentive-based tool that permits a developer to increase the
maximum allowable development density on a site in exchange for specified public policy
goals. If adopted, the proposed Ordinance would provide density bonuses to help develop
affordable housing units in exchange for a menu of incentives to make development
easier. This is accomplished by reducing the applicable development standards such as
height, floor area ratio, and setbacks, among others.

Density bonus regulations are mandated by Government Code § 65915. The City’s
density bonus regulations were last updated in 2013 and there have been changes in
California law during the last ten years that require amendments to the MPMC. The
proposed Ordinance will reconcile the City’s regulations with applicable law.

ANALYSIS

If adopted, the Ordinance will implement Government Code §§ 65915, et seq.
(Attachment A). Currently, California law permits a bonus ranging from 20-80% density
increase, depending on how many affordable housing units the developer includes in a
project. Additionally, for projects that provide 100% affordable units, applicants are
allowed unlimited density bonus and an additional three stories of building height if
located near a major transit stop. Under the State law, the following are the minimum
thresholds that qualify a project for a density bonus:

    5% of units set-aside for very low income households;
    10% of units set-aside for lower income households ;
    10% of for-sale units set-aside for moderate income households ;

  Page 131 of 356
 Staff Report
Page 3 of 4
June 7, 2023

    100% of units set-aside for very low, low-, and moderate-income households (with
  maximum 20% moderate);
    10% of the housing units set-aside for transitional foster youth, disabled veterans
  or homeless persons, with rents restricted at the very low-income level;
    20% of units set-aside for low-income college students in housing dedicated for
  full-time students at accredited colleges;
    The project dedicates at least one acre of land, or land of sufficient size to permit
  at least 40 units, to the city for very low-income units and is appropriately zoned
  and includes access to public utilities and infrastructure;
    The project is a senior citizen housing development with at least 35 units (no
  affordable units required); and
    The project is a mobile home park this is age-restricted to senior citizens (no
  affordable units required)

As part of the update to the Density Bonus regulations, an updated menu of incentives is
included. This allows the City to prioritize relaxation of development standards. The menu
of incentives provides clarity to developers while preserving the City’s interests and
priorities. The menu of incentives includes:

    Reduction of yards and setbacks;
    Reduction of lot width requirements;
    Increase of floor area ratio;

   I. INTRODUCTION

  This Monterey Park Market Place Specific Plan (Specific Plan) was prepared in conformity with
  Government Code § 65451, et seq. Together with zoning regulations adopted by the Monterey
  Park Municipal Code (MPMC) and other Applicable Law (defined below), this Specific Plan sets
  forth the regulations for the development and operation of the Monterey Park Market Place
  project (Project or the Market Place).

  Pursuant to Government Code § 65450, a specific plan must include text and a diagram or
  diagrams, which specify all of the following in detail:

  •  The distribution, location, and extent of the uses of land, including open space within the
  area covered by the plan.
  •  The proposed distribution, location, extent, and intensity of major components of public
  and private transportation, sewage, water, drainage, solid waste disposal, energy and
  other essential facilities proposed to be located within the land area covered by the plan
  and needed to support the land uses described in the plan.
  •  Standards and criteria by which development will proceed, and standards for the
  conservation, development, and utilization of natural resources, where applicable.
  •  A program of implementation measures, including regulations, programs, public works
  projects and financing measures necessary to carry out the above items.
  •  A discussion of the relationship of the Specific Plan to the General Plan.

  This Specific Plan is compatible and consistent with the goals and policies outlined in the City of
  Monterey Park’s General Plan (General Plan). This Specific Plan will further the goals and policies
  of the General Plan as more fully described below.

  This Specific Plan was prepared to provide the essential relationship between the policies of the
  General Plan and actual development in the Project area. By functioning as a regulatory
  document, the Specific Plan provides a means of implementing the General Plan. All future
  development within the Specific Plan boundaries must be consistent with the standards set forth
  in this document.

A.  SPECIFIC PLAN AREA
  This Specific Plan regulates real property (a triangular-shaped parcel consisting of approximately
  63.68 acres) located in the southeast portion of the City of Monterey Park, in the County of Los
  Angeles, State of California, immediately north of the Pomona Freeway, State Route 60 (Pomona
  Freeway), and west of Paramount Boulevard as shown on Figure 1 (Specific Plan Area).

   II. SPECIFIC PLAN OVERVIEW

A.  PURPOSE AND AUTHORITY OF THE SPECIFIC PLAN
  This Specific Plan is intended to provide for the orderly and efficient development of the Specific
  Plan Area in accordance with the provisions of the General Plan. In conjunction with the General
  Plan, the Specific Plan implements the plan for the physical development of the Specific Plan Area
  and a guide to all future development within the plan area.

  A Specific Plan may be prepared for any defined geographic area, which might benefit from
  specialized land use regulations and development standards.

  The Specific Plan provides for development within the Specific Plan Area and establishes the
  permitted uses, development intensity, site planning and development standards, design and
  architecture, landscaping, signs, refuse facilities, access and circulation, parking, and trip
  reduction measures of the Project.

B.  SPECIFIC PLAN SCOPE AND GOALS
  Implementation of General Plan goals and policies will occur through the establishment of land
  use designations, traffic circulation patterns, development policies, and the identification of
  backbone infrastructure necessary to support the planned intensity of development.

  To achieve this purpose, the Specific Plan has the following goals:

  1. Establish the planning concept, design theme, development regulations, and procedures
  necessary to achieve an orderly and compatible development;
  2. Implement the goals, policies, and objectives of the General Plan;
  3. Establish a framework to create a successful Project with a mix of predominantly retail
  uses with retail-supporting uses, such as Last Mile Distribution Center and Warehouse
  uses;
  4. Meet changing market demands for more home delivery by allowing car sales, Last Mile
  Distribution Center and Warehouse uses;
  5. Facilitate the full build-out of the Specific Plan Area; and
  6. Provide clear design guidelines and standards to allow for flexibility in the implementation
  and build-out of planned development within the Specific Plan area.

  6

 C.  CONSISTENCY WITH THE GENERAL PLAN
  The General Plan serves as the long-term planning guide for future development throughout the
  City. The General Plan operates as a guide to the type of community desired for the future and
  provides the means to accomplish that goal. California Law and the MPMC require a Specific Plan
  to be consistent with the General Plan. This Specific Plan is consistent with the General Plan and
  advances the goals and policies identified below.

  1. Land Use Element: The Specific Plan is consistent with the Land Use and Urban Design
  Element of the General Plan and the following goals and policies:
  •  Goal 1: Commercial districts that allow a variety of retail, service, and entertainment
  uses and that accommodate flexibility over time.
  •  Policy 1.1: Flexibility. Ensure zoning regulations provide flexibility regarding allowed
  uses.
  •  Goal 2: Dynamic mix of businesses, uses, and employment that sustains a strong local
  economy and contributes to a fiscally sustainable tax base.
  •  Policy 2.1: Flexibility. Provide flexible and clear development standards to allow
  commercial, professional, industrial, institutional, and hospitality businesses and uses
  to expand and thrive economically.
  •  Policy 2.2: Business Growth. Facilitate the growth of a diverse business sector resilient
  to change over time and compatible with a broad range of skills and workers.
  •  Goal 12: High design quality in all new commercial developments and rehabilitation
  projects.
  •  Policy 12.1: Compatibility. Require new, infill, and rehabilitation projects in
  commercial districts be compatible with existing contexts in terms of site design,
  scale, building design, materials, and architectural approaches.
  •  Policy 12.2: Comprehensive Design. Provide for comprehensive design review of new
  commercial development.
  •  Goal 14: The Market Place as a regional destination for diverse shopping, dining and
  entertainment experiences.
  •  Policy 14.1: Flexibility. Ensure that zoning regulations applicable to the Market Place
  properties provide focus for the uses the City looks to attract, while providing
  ﬂexibility to accommodate emerging new uses and markets over time.
  •  Policy 14.2: Traffic. Work with property owners and property managers to address and
  manage traffic associated with the Market Place, so that visitors avoid traveling
  through adjacent residential neighborhoods.

   •  Policy 14.3: High Design Quality. Insist upon high design quality and landscape

The land uses allowed under the Specific Plan are consistent with the Land Use Policy Map

A.  DEVELOPMENT CONCEPT
  The Specific Plan provides a framework for developing approximately 63.68-acres in the
  southeast portion of Monterey Park and an additional nine-acre area of easements owned by
  SCE. The development is a highway oriented commercial project consisting of approximately
  600,000 square feet of commercial uses and/or distribution and warehouse uses, with adequate
  supporting parking spaces and associated landscaping, inclusive of existing and proposed

   development within the Specific Plan Area. Collectively, the Specific Plan Area and SCE easement
  areas are referred to as the “Site.”

  Development may be based on four Conceptual Development Plans, set forth in Section V.D.2,
  below, or as otherwise allowed under the Specific Plan.

  Build-out of the Specific Plan would provide a range of economic, fiscal, and quality of life benefits
  to the City.

B.  LAND USE PLAN
  This Specific Plan provides a framework of infrastructure and urban design that will
  accommodate the wide range of commercial/industrial uses anticipated over the life of the
  Project while remaining consistent with Monterey Park’s suburban character.

  New development of Individual Projects may be based on one of the Conceptual Development
  Plans (see Figures 4A, 4B, 4C, and 4D). Development options other than the Conceptual
  Development Plans are permissible as set forth in the Specific Plan.

C.  GRADING CONCEPT
  Grading plans for an Individual Project’s building pads, roadways, pedestrian paths, water, sewer,
  and other utilities will be developed as needed for each Individual Project. Grading may consist
  of over excavation of soils beneath proposed buildings, to a depth of three to four feet, to remove
  unsuitable building material.

  Limited import for Individual Projects may be necessary, and is permissible, to stabilize soils
  depending upon the final geotechnical recommendations of a soils engineer.

  All grading must be accomplished pursuant to a Grading Plan that contains the following:

  a. Best management practices (BMPs).
  b. Non-paved areas must be revegetated or restored promptly after installation of utilities
  using drought-resistant, fast-growing vegetation that would quickly stabilize exposed
  ground surfaces. Alternative materials rather than reseeding (e.g., gravel) may be used in
  accordance with the Director’s direction.
  c. Runoff must be conveyed in accordance with the approved site drainage plans.
  d. Energy dissipaters or similar devices may be required at the end of drainpipe outlets to
  minimize erosion during storm events.
  e. Grading cannot occur during the wet season (November 1-April 15) unless erosion control
  devices acceptable to the City are implemented.

   f. Grading must be completed such that permanent drainage away from foundations and
  slabs is provided and so that water does not pond near proposed structures or

  but may include roadways, utility infrastructure, loading, parking, landscaping, and fences
  and walls.

  configurations and a minimum of 12-foot widths for one-way configurations. Parking area

  area. All such parking stalls must be located reasonably near the storefronts for easy

  6. Compact Spaces – The Site may include compact parking spaces. Compact spaces are
  those reduced from the standard 9’ x 18’ to 7 ‘ 6 “ x 16’. Compact stalls may not total

  spaces and that contain more than 50,000 square feet of floor area. Truck loading bays or

  have their own waste management areas within their building footprints to maintain the proper
  visual aesthetics of the Specific Plan Area. Public waste management will be accomplished by

  implemented to the maximum extent feasible:
  a. Off-site locations for construction waste exported from the Site and options for
  disposal of excess material should be identified. These options may include recycling
  of materials on-Site, sale to a broker or contractor, sale to a project in the vicinity, or
  transport to an environmentally cleared landfill.

  implemented, to the maximum extent feasible, by the Project tenants within their
  buildings and will be specified in lease agreements between the Applicant and individual
  tenants:
  a. Recovery of materials such as aluminum and cardboard;
  b. Collection of office paper for recycling;

  The Director must confirm that the number of a.m., p.m., and Saturday peak hour and daily trips
  for a proposed Individual Project, based on a trip generation memorandum prepared by the
  Applicant’s transportation engineer, to determine whether or not such trips would cause the Trip
  Cap to be cumulatively exceeded. The Applicant may receive a trip credit for an existing or
  previous entitlement and/or use that was or will be discontinued.

  Trips for an Individual Project having more than one use will be calculated by adding together the
  trips generated by the portion of floor area of the Project devoted to each use unless the Director,
  based on reasonable methods, determines otherwise.

  The Applicant’s trip generation memorandum will be based on the then-current Institute of
  Transportation Engineers (ITE) Trip Generation Handbook, or such alternative rates determined
  to be appropriate by the Applicant’s transportation engineer and approved by the Director. The
  determination of trips will reflect diverted and pass-by traffic trips, the effect of interaction of
  on-site mixed-use development, the proximity of the Project to mass transit facilities, and
  implementation of other transportation demand management measures.

  If the Director disagrees with any of the trip generation factors as applied to an Individual Project,
  the Applicant may submit a proposed alternative trip generation factor for the Project, along with
  a traffic generation study prepared by transportation engineer, for review by the Planning
  Agency. Upon receiving such a study from the Applicant, the Director will cause the City Clerk to
  schedule a public hearing before the Monterey Park Planning Agency in accordance with the
  MPMC. Within 45 days after conducting a public hearing, the Planning Agency will issue written

  change the effect of any regulation, or (ii) changes to a Conceptual Plan that are in
  substantial conformance with the Specific Plan.
  b. Changes in any Specific Plan Area boundary.
  c. Increases in the specified density for the Specific Plan Area, except as expressly
  authorized under the Specific Plan.
  d. Increases in Trip Caps.
  e. Changes in standards or regulations, including landscaping and design standards,
  except to the extent the changes constitute a Minor Modification, as set forth in
  MPMC § 21.32.030.

C.  ADMINISTRATIVE MODIFICATIONS
  1. The Director is authorized to make technical corrections, in a form approved by the City
  Attorney, to maps, diagrams, tables, and other similar documents that may be required
  to reconcile the changes made by this Specific Plan and Applicable Law.
  2. In addition, the Director is authorized to make the following technical amendments, in a
  form approved by the City Attorney:
  a. Realignment or modifications to internal streets serving the project, lot lines,
  easement locations, and grading adjustments, if approved by the City Engineer.
  b. Minor modification to design criteria such as paving treatments, architectural details,
  and related criteria.
  c. Minor modification to landscape treatments, fencing, lighting, pedestrian paths, and
  entry treatments, provided the modifications are in substantial conformance with the

 1.  Introduction
1.1  PURPOSE OF MITIGATION MONITORING PROGRAM

This Mitigation Monitoring Program has been developed to provide a vehicle by which to monitor mitigation
measures and conditions of approval outlined in the 2000 Monterey Park Towne Plaza (MPTP) EIR, the
Supplemental Environmental Impact Report (Draft SEIR), and the Final Supplemental EIR (Final SEIR) (State
Clearinghouse No. 1999051058). The Mitigation Monitoring Program has been prepared in conformance with
Section 21081.6 of the Public Resources Code and City of Monterey Park Monitoring Requirements. Section
21081.6 states:

  (a) When making findings required by paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 21081 or
  when adopting a mitigated negative declaration pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision
  (c) of Section 21080, the following requirements shall apply:

  (1) The public agency shall adopt a reporting or monitoring program for the changes
  made to the project or conditions of project approval, adopted in order to mitigate or
  avoid significant effects on the environment. The reporting or monitoring program
  shall be designed to ensure compliance during project implementation. For those
  changes which have been required or incorporated into the project at the request of
  a responsible agency or a public agency having jurisdiction by law over natural
  resources affected by the project, that agency shall, if so requested by the lead or
  responsible agency, prepare and submit a proposed reporting or monitoring
  program.

  (2) The lead agency shall specify the location and custodian of the documents or other
  material which constitute the record of proceedings upon which its decision is
  based.

The Mitigation Monitoring Program will serve to document compliance with adopted/certified mitigation
measures, which are formulated to minimize impacts associated with the construction and operation of the
revised Monterey Park Market Place project (proposed project).

1.2  EIR SUMMARY

1.2.1  Previously Proposed 2000 Monterey Park Towne Plaza Site Plan

In March 2000, the Final EIR/EIS for the previous project was certified by the City of Monterey Park Planning
Commission. The City had the principal responsibility for project approval and acted as the CEQA lead
agency as defined by Section 15367 of the CEQA Guidelines. To help with the costs of land acquisition, site
cleanup, and required access, the City received a Section 108 Loan Guarantee and an accompanying
Economic Development Initiative grant from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).
Because of the assistance provided by HUD, the project was subject to National Environmental Protection Act
(NEPA) review, and HUD was the federal (NEPA) lead agency for the previous project.

The previous site plan required the demolition of all existing buildings, excluding the LTP, and the leveling of
the berm along SR-60 on the southern portion of the site. Contaminated berm soil (with traces of lead) would
be removed from the site while the remaining soil would be used to level the site. The previously proposed

Based on the type of commercial business and the various buildout options, anchor stores, including the
garden centers, would make up a maximum of 561,011 square feet, nonanchor retail would make up 3,225 to
22,989 square feet, and restaurants would make up 16,000 to 35,764 square feet of the total gross building
area.

Although not included with the proposed project, a leachate treatment plant (LTP) and thermal destruction
facility (TDF) will continue to operate on the project site. Leachate is a common product of landfills, made of
groundwater and the compounds of decomposing material in the landfill. The LTP collects leachate from the
south parcel of the OII landfill and treats it. Off-gas is produced during leachate treatment and must be burned
in the treatment plant. The LTP directs off-gas to the South Parcel via a 12-inch pipeline, where it is burned
along with gas produced in the South Parcel. The TDF structure has two 60-foot high stacks, each
approximately 6 feet in diameter. It was constructed after the certification of the 2000 MPTP EIR and
improves the leachate treatment process. The structure would be contained by a chain-link fence and public
access would be restricted.

 1. Introduction

Monterey Park Market Place Precise Plan

The proposed project includes the Monterey Park Market Place (MPMP) Precise Plan, which is a required
document for development within the Regional-Specialty Center (R-S) Planned Development Overlay Zone to
ensure consistency with the Monterey Park General Plan. The purpose of having a precise plan is to describe
how the proposed project would meet the requirements of the Planned Development Overlay Zone on the
project site; provide the overall design concept for the site; implement the goals, policies, and objectives of
the City’s general plan as feasible; and establish the development regulations and framework for the project
site.

Detailed building and site development standards and regulations are included in the precise plan, such as
architectural themes, building height, and types of permitted businesses. Maximum height of buildings is set
in the MPMP Precise Plan and meets the standards of the R-S Planned Development Zone Overlay, which is
50 feet or 4 stories. Architectural features are allowed to project an additional 15 feet above maximum
building height with the approval of a conditional use permit. The proposed buildings would be between 30
and 50 feet in height (up to 60 feet with architectural features).

Project Access and Parking

The existing access road for the proposed project site is Greenwood Avenue, which enters the northern
boundary of the project site from Potrero Grande Drive. The main road through the development would be
named Market Place Drive. This road would be slightly realigned where it enters the project site on the north
and then extended toward the east corner of the site. Neil Armstrong Street would no longer intersect
Paramount Avenue but would intersect Market Place Drive instead. Market Place Drive would intersect
Paramount Avenue east of the project site. With the completion of all roadway improvements, the site would
be accessible from both Potrero Grande Drive and Paramount Boulevard off of SR-60.

Market Place Drive would serve as the main public/private roadway through the retail center and it would
allow truck and standard vehicle access. Additional specified truck/service routes would allow access to the
buildings to allow for pick-up and delivery of goods. The circulation plan for the project site will identify the
primary vehicle, truck/service, and pedestrian access routes on the project site.

Onsite parking is provided based on the parking demand ratio of the proposed land uses per 1,000 square
feet of building space, as shown in the far right column in Table 1. A minimum of 2,333 spaces would be
provided, including 44 handicapped spaces throughout the site, placed near the entrances for anchor stores,
the smaller mixed retail/restaurant stores, and the retail/restaurant pads. Although 2,333 are required, up to
2,386 would be provided, which would result in a surplus of up to 53 parking spaces. All parking lots are
aboveground surface lots and would be accessible from Market Place Drive.

Alternate Land Use Scenario: Small-Box Development

An alternative layout to the revised project is also provided for the project site in the event that the project
applicant opts to develop a small-box retail shopping center instead of the big-box retail. The small-box
alternative would have a reduced total square footage of 500,000 square feet that would include 3 anchors,
up to 10 smaller retail stores, and 7 retail pads. The retail anchor stores would line the northern boundary of
the project site and retail anchor “E” (110,000 square feet) would have a garden center (30,000 square feet).
The largest anchor, Retail A (140,000 square feet), would be north of the northern Greenwood Avenue
(Market Place Drive) entrance. South of Retail A, across Market Place Drive, are Retail stores G through M.
Retail F, which is adjacent to the LTP/TDF, Retail Pad 6, and Retail Pad 7 are all more centrally located on
the site and Retail B and C and Retail Pads 1 through 5 share the northern boundary of the site with the
anchor stores. Anchor stores would have a total square footage of 321,000, and retail nonanchor stores
would have a total square footage between 139,000 and 150,000, depending on whether Retail F is

1.3  PROJECT LOCATION

The proposed Monterey Park Market Place is in the southern portion of the City of Monterey Park and borders
the City of Montebello. It would be at 2550 Greenwood Avenue, north of SR-60 between the Paramount
Boulevard and Potrero Grande Drive freeway exits. The project site is bounded by Southern California Edison
(SCE) easements on the northwest and northeast. Beyond the SCE easements are Potrero Grande Drive to

This document has been prepared as a supplement to a previous Environmental Impact Report as defined by
the State CEQA Guidelines (Section 15163, California Code of Regulations, Title 14, Division 6, Chapter 3).
Specifically, a supplement to the certified EIR has been prepared for the 2000 Monterey Park Towne Plaza
(SCH No. 1999051058). The Draft SEIR has an overall purpose to inform the lead agency, responsible
agencies, decision makers, and the general public of the environmental effects of the development and
operation of the revised project. The Draft SEIR addressed the potential environmental effects of the revised
project, including effects that might be significant and adverse; disclosed effects not found to be significant;
disclosed significant cumulative impacts of all past, present, and reasonably foreseeable future projects;
evaluated a number of alternatives to the revised project; and identified mitigation measures to reduce or
avoid adverse effects.

1.4.3  Unavoidable Significant Adverse Impacts

With mitigation measures, air quality, greenhouse gas emissions, and transportation and traffic would have
significant and unavoidable impacts

Air Quality

Impact 5.2-2

Construction emissions exceed SCAQMD’s regional significance thresholds for NOx and would cumulatively
contribute to the SoCAB’s nonattainment designations. Grading emissions would be roughly the same
between the 2000 MPTP EIR and the revised MPMP Precise Plan. However, the 2000 MPTP EIR did not
identify significant construction emissions because construction activities were compared to screening
thresholds and were not modeled. SCAQMD now requires comparison to daily emissions thresholds and new
air pollutant models (e.g., URBEMIS) have been released to evaluate construction emissions. Modeling
results now show that even with implementation of Mitigation Measures 2-1 and 2-7, impacts from regional air
pollutant emissions from construction-related activities would exceed SCAQMD’s regional significance
thresholds for NOX as a result of use of heavy construction equipment. Mitigation Measure 2-7 would reduce
potentially significant impacts during Phase 1 construction activities to under the significance thresholds;
however, construction activities during Phase 2 site preparation would continue to exceed SCAQMD’s
regional significance thresholds for NOX. Therefore, impacts are significant and unavoidable. Regional
construction emissions impacts are a new significant unavoidable impact not identified in the 2000 MPTP EIR.

Impact 5.2-3

Operational phase emissions exceed SCAQMD’s regional significance thresholds for VOC, NOX, CO, PM10,
and PM2.5 and would cumulatively contribute to the SoCAB’s nonattainment designations. The MPMP Precise
Plan would exceed the thresholds for VOC, CO, NOX, PM10, and PM2.5. Mitigation Measures 2-8 through 2-17
would reduce operational emissions, to the extent feasible. Criteria air pollutant emissions that exceed
SCAQMD’s regional significance thresholds would cumulatively contribute to the NO 2, O3, and particulate
matter nonattainment designations of the SoCAB. While air quality impacts were identified in the 2000 MPTP
EIR, the MPMP Precise Plan would result in an approximately 5 to 8 percent increase in air quality impacts for
most criteria pollutants on weekdays and an approximately 44 percent increase in air quality impacts for most
criteria pollutants on weekends, compared to the 2000 MPTP. However, the project would result in a
decrease in air quality impacts based on emissions as identified in the 2000 MPTP EIR for CO (weekday
only), VOC, and NOx because of updated emission rates used in this SEIR that reflect lower emission rates
for vehicles. Further, based on the updated emission factors in the UREMIS2007 model, the revised SEIR
analysis has identified additional significant impacts associated with PM10 and PM2.5 that were not identified in
the EIR. The increase in air pollutant emissions would exceed the SCAQMD regional thresholds and therefore
the magnitude of change is considered to be significant. Modeling based on updated air pollutant emission
factors in the URBEMIS2007 model show that VOC, CO, NOX, PM10, and PM2.5 would exceed the significance
thresholds for the MPMP Precise Plan. Since emissions of particulate matter (PM 10 and PM2.5) were not

 2.  Mitigation Monitoring Process
2.1  MITIGATION MONITORING PROGRAM ORGANIZATION

CEQA requires that a reporting or monitoring program be adopted for the conditions of project approval that
are necessary to mitigate or avoid significant effects on the environment (Public Resources Code 21081.6).
The mitigation monitoring and reporting program is designed to ensure compliance with adopted mitigation
measures during project implementation. For each mitigation measure recommended in the Environmental
Impact Report, specifications are made herein that identify the action required and the monitoring that must
occur. In addition, a responsible agency is identified for verifying compliance with individual conditions of
approval contained in the Mitigation Monitoring Program (MMP). In order to effectively track and document
the status of mitigation measures, a mitigation matrix has been prepared and includes:

    Responsibility for implementation
    Timing
    Responsibility for monitoring
    Monitor

Mitigation measure timing of verification has been apportioned into several specific timing increments. Of
these, the most common are:

    Prior to project approval
    Prior to issuance of grading permit(s)
    During construction

Information pertaining to compliance with mitigation measures or any necessary modifications or refinements
will be documented in the comments portion of the matrix.

Supplement to the Certified 2000 EIR Mitigation Monitoring Program

Since this is a supplemental EIR, the MMP for this project modifies the previously adopted MMP for the
Monterey Park Towne Plaza (March 2000). The MMP for the SEIR includes the revised and new mitigation
measures for the proposed project. Where appropriate, the timing and responsible agency information from
the 2000 MMP has been retained.

2.2  MITIGATION MONITORING PROCEDURES

The City of Monterey Park Development Services Department is the designated lead agency for the Mitigation
Monitoring and Reporting Program. The City of Monterey Park includes the Mitigation Measures within the
Special Conditions of Approval. The City is responsible for review of all monitoring reports, enforcement
actions, and document disposition. The Community Development Department shall designate a Project
Mitigation Monitor for the proposed project.

2.2.1  In-Field Monitoring

The Responsible Monitoring Party shall exercise caution and professional practices at all times when
monitoring construction. Protective wear (hard hats, glasses, etc.) shall be worn at all times in construction
areas. Injuries shall be reported immediately to the Project Mitigation Monitor.

2.2.2  Coordination with Contractors

The construction manager/superintendent is responsible for coordination of contractors and for contractor
completion of required measures in accordance with the provisions of this program.

2.2.3  Recognized Experts

The use of recognized experts as a component of the monitoring team is required to ensure compliance with
scientific and engineering mitigation measures. While the recognized experts assess compliance with
required mitigation measures, consultation with the City of Monterey Park planning staff shall take place in the
event of a dispute.

2.2.4  Enforcement

Agencies may enforce conditions of approval through their existing police power, using stop-work orders,
fines, infraction citations, loss of entitlements, refusal to issue building permits or certificates of use and
occupancy or, in some cases, notice of violation for tax purposes. Criminal misdemeanor sanctions could be
available where the agency has adopted an ordinance requiring compliance with the monitoring program,
similar to the provision in many zoning ordinances that affirm the enforcement power to bring suit against
violators of the ordinances.

3.1  CATEGORIZED MITIGATION MEASURES/MATRIX

Project-specific mitigation measures and project design features (PDFs) have been categorized in matrix
format, as shown in Table 3-1. The matrix identifies the environmental factor, specific mitigation measures,
schedule, and responsible monitor. The mitigation matrix will serve as the basis for scheduling the
implementation of, and compliance with, all mitigation measures.

A supplemental EIR only discusses new environmental impacts that would result from a change in the project
description between the original and revised projects and it only needs to contain the information necessary to
make the previous EIR adequate for the project as revised (CEQA Guidelines Section 15163). To avoid
certain environmental impacts, the City of Monterey Park has included certain PDFs, which are considered
part of the proposed project. The PDFs are mandatory and will be adopted by the City of Monterey Park as
part of the project’s conditions of approval. Both the PDFs and mitigation measures are part of the MMP to
be implemented by the City of Monterey Park. To provide a complete matrix that may be used for monitoring
and enforcement, this mitigation monitoring program includes mitigation measures and project design
features associated with the new impacts caused by the proposed project, as well as all mitigation measures
which remain effective from the previously certified 2000 MPTP EIR.

3.2  LONG-TERM MONITORING

Long-term monitoring related to several mitigation measures will be required, including fire safety inspections.
Postconstruction fire inspections are conducted on a routine basis by the City of Monterey Park Fire
Department.

 4.  Mitigation Monitoring Reports
Mitigation monitoring reports are required to document compliance with the Mitigation Monitoring Program
and to dispute arbitration enforcement resolution. Specific reports include:

    Field Check Report
    Implementation Compliance Report
    Arbitration/Enforcement Report

4.1  FIELD CHECK REPORT

Field check reports are required to record in-field compliance and conditions.

4.2  IMPLEMENTATION COMPLIANCE REPORT

The Implementation Compliance Report (ICR) is prepared to document the implementation of mitigation
measures on a phased basis, based on the information in Table 3-1. The report summarizes implementation
compliance, including mitigation measures, date completed, and monitor’s signature.

4.3  ARBITRATION/ENFORCEMENT REPORT

The Arbitration/Enforcement Report (AER) is prepared to document the outcome of arbitration committee
review and becomes a portion of the ICR.

  Municipal Code (“MPMC”) § 21.32.070.

On September 16, 2021, Monterey Park Retail Partners Tract 3, LLC, submitted a request
for a conditional use permit (“CUP”) to add a fourth drive through restaurant at the Market
Place development that the City Council approved December 19, 2012 (the “Project”).
The Market Place Precise Plan allowed up to three drive-through restaurants be approved
ministerially; any subsequent drive-throughs require a CUP. The general layout, uses,
parking, and traffic patterns are all the same as originally contemplated by the City Council
on December 19, 2012.

The Project is considered a “project” under the California Environmental Quality Act
(“CEQA”). Accordingly, environmental review is required pursuant to CEQA (Public
Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq.) and the CEQA Guidelines (14 Cal. Code of
Regulations §§ 15000, et seq.).

Background

On December 19, 2012, the Monterey Park City Council adopted Resolution No. 11548
certifying the Final Supplemental Environmental Impact Report (SEIR) for the Market
Place project and adopting a Statement of Overriding Considerations (see Final EIR/EIS
at State Clearinghouse No. 1999051058). Implementation of mitigation measures
identified in the SEIR will be monitored as called for in the Mitigation Monitoring and
Reporting Program adopted on December 19, 2012.

The circumstances, impacts, and mitigation requirements identified in the SEIR remain
applicable to the proposed Project; there are no new issues and the level of environmental
impacts identified in the SEIR is static.

Environmental Analysis

CEQA Guidelines § 15168(c)(2) states that if a project is proposed which has been the
subject of a prior certified EIR, and “[i]f the [City] finds that pursuant to Section 15162, no
new effects could occur or new mitigation measures would be required, the agency can
approve the activity as being within the scope of the project covered by the … EIR, and
no new environmental document would be required.”
CEQA Guidelines § 15162 defines the conditions under which a subsequent EIR would
be required for a project as follows:
 (1)  Substantial changes are proposed in the project which require major revisions of
  the EIR due to the involvement of new significant environmental effects or

  Page 273 of 356
   substantial increase in the severity of previously identified significant effects;
 (2)  Substantial changes occur with respect to the circumstances under which the
  project is undertaken which will require major revisions of the previous EIR due to
  involvement of new significant environmental effects or a substantial increase in
  the severity of previously identified significant effects; and/or
 (3)  New information of substantial importance, which was not known and could not
  have been known with the exercise of reasonable diligence at the time the previous
  EIR was adopted, shows any of the following:
  1. The revised project will have one or more significant effects not discussed in
  the previous EIR;
  2. Significant effects previously examined will be substantially more severe than
  shown in the previous EIR;
  3. Mitigation measures or alternatives previously found not to be feasible would
  in fact be feasible and would substantially reduce one or more significant
  effects of the project, but the project proponents decline to adopt the mitigation
  measure or alternative; or
  4. Mitigation measures or alternatives which are considerably different from those
  analyzed in the previous EIR would substantially reduce one or more significant
  effects on the environment, but the project proponents decline to adopt the
  mitigation measure or alternative.

As stated above, the Project will not result in any new environmental effect not
already considered in the SEIR.

Findings

Based on the above analysis, the City Council of Monterey Park makes the following
findings:

1. On December 19, 2012, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 11548 and certified
  a Supplemental EIR for the project.
2. The Project will not facilitate the creation of any development beyond that anticipated
  and accounted for by the certified Supplemental EIR.
3. Approval of the Project will not result in any new or increased environmental effects,
  and no new mitigation measures are required.
4. Pursuant to CEQA Guidelines § 15168(c)(2), no new environmental documentation is
  required for approval of the Project.

Chapter 21.44 of the MPMC requires Development Agreements (DA) for large scale
projects that require multiple entitlements and long-term commitment of both public and

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
Beginning in January 2023 Chinatown Service Center (CSC) spearheaded the efforts to
assist with the mental health and wellness of community members following the January
21, 2023 mass shooting at the Star Ballroom dance studio.

In March 2023 Chinatown Service Center was invited to apply for the Antiterrorism
Emergency Assistance Program (AEAP) grant from the Federal Office for Victims of
Crime (OVC) to fund the establishment of a Community Resiliency Center to serve the
victims and community members affected by the incident. This grant guarantees
Resiliency Center funding to affected communities, however disbursement is not
immediate and it can take up to 18 months for agencies to receive funds.

Chinatown Service Center is seeking a location for a temporary Community Resiliency
Center while they work on identifying a permanent location. City staff have worked with
CSC to find potential City facilities to house a temporary Community Resiliency Center
and have identified the Sierra Vista Community Center as a site.

The City would like to execute a license agreement with Chinatown Service Center for
use of the Sierra Vista Community Center until December 31, 2023. As part of the

license agreement, the City will provide the space for Chinatown Service Center to
provide individual and group therapy, wellness activities, tai chi and meditation and
other activities for the community.

Staff is recommending City Council authorize the City Manager, or designee, to execute
a license agreement, in a form approved by the City Attorney, to use the Sierra Vista
Community Center to provide a temporary Community Resiliency Center.

BACKGROUND:
In March 2023 Chinatown Service Center was invited to apply for the Antiterrorism
Emergency Assistance Program grant by consultants of the Federal government with
the Office for Victims of Crime (OVC). AEAP grants are available by OVC invitation
only. Shortly after an event, OVC will contact officials in the jurisdiction where the
incident occurred to discuss the scope of victims’ needs and explain what resources
may be available. These grants are offered to communities where mass casualty
incidents have occurred and provide funding for resources and services to victims and
residents beyond the acute phase of an incident in the form of a Community Resiliency
Center.

The Office for Victims of Crime describes the purpose of a Community Resiliency
Center as, “providing a safe and supportive healing environment for affected individuals
and groups seeking to improve their emotional and physical health related to the trauma
they experienced due to a mass violence incident.”

Since the invitation, CSC conducted four large community stakeholder meetings and
many additional meetings with individuals and organizations to gather information in
order to complete a needs assessment for a Community Resiliency Center. Through
these meetings, CSC concluded the Resiliency Center will best serve the community
with the following core services: counseling (individual and group), outreach and
engagement, wellness workshops and community activities. Special attention has also
been given to healing practices of the diverse faith communities in Monterey Park and
the surrounding areas such as Buddhist meditation, chanting and walking meditation.

CSC will lead the Resiliency Center operations and manage the core services identified.
CSC anticipates that the operations of the Resiliency Center and the services offered
will evolve and adapt according to the community’s needs.

City staff and elected officials have been involved in the stakeholder meetings since
their inception and have worked with CSC to identify a potential space within the City
that meets their needs for a temporary center. Staff will also assist with identifying
vacant commercial spaces in the City for a more long-term solution.

The ideal square footage is around 3,000 square feet and the space should
accommodate the following operations:

  •  Individual rooms for therapy
  •  Multipurpose spaces to accommodate groups programs of at least 25 attendees
  •  An office space for staff to manage operations and the facility
  •  An outdoor space for activities such as yoga and tai chi
  •  Storage space for supplies and materials
  •  An optional kitchen space

In late May, staff from CSC and the City toured two City facilities, El Encanto and the
Sierra Vista Community Center, and identified the Sierra Vista Community Center as a
potential temporary space for the MPK Hope Resiliency Center. The Sierra Vista
Community Center measures 2,416 square feet and meets most of the needs identified
by CSC. It has outdoor space, an office, storage space, a multipurpose space that can
be split with an accordion wall, and public restroom facilities.

Following the identification of the Sierra Vista Community Center as a potential location,
Chinatown Service Center also provided a draft budget of their total operational costs
for the first 20 months of the Resiliency Center. Estimated costs included staffing and
benefits, travel, supplies, contracts, utilities, outreach, promotion, and insurance costs
for Chinatown Service Center to operate the Resiliency Center.

The current market rate of commercial space in Monterey Park is $2.21 per square foot,

This cost would also include utilities for the building, landscaping costs, security
cameras, and facility maintenance as in-kind contributions. The City can also offer use

promotional assistance through City media channels to help offset start-up costs.

Chinatown Service Center is currently writing the Antiterrorism and Emergency

Community Resiliency Center at market rate. However, the disbursement of funds may

Council may elect to postpone collection of the rental and janitorial costs of the Sierra
